title: How the body fights infection
specPoints: Year 9 bridging: barriers, white blood cells, immunity, vaccines and antibiotics

tips.title: Mucus traps, cilia sweep
tips.body: Two cells, two jobs. The **mucus** is sticky and **traps** what you breathe in; the **cilia** beat and **move** the mucus to the throat. Giving the trapping job to the cilia is the commonest lost mark on barriers. Smoke stops the cilia, which is why the mucus, and the infections, build up.

tips.title: Phagocyte or lymphocyte?
tips.body: If the question says **engulfs**, **digests** or **any pathogen**, it wants **phagocyte**. If it says **antibody**, **antigen**, **specific** or **memory**, it wants **lymphocyte**. Pus points to phagocytes; immunity points to lymphocytes.

tips.title: The four anti-words
tips.body: Before you write one, ask who has it. On the **pathogen**: antigen. Made by **your lymphocytes**: antibody. A **medicine** against bacteria: antibiotic. For **skin and surfaces**: antiseptic. A wrong anti-word is marked as wrong, however good the sentence round it.

tips.title: A vaccine gives memory, not antibodies
tips.body: The vaccine's antigens make your own lymphocytes respond and leave **memory cells**. Antibody levels fade within months; memory cells stay for years. That is why a vaccine works long after any antibodies it triggered have gone.

tips.title: Virus in the question, structure in the answer
tips.body: Whenever a question pairs a **virus** with an **antibiotic**, the answer is the same: a virus is **not a cell**, so there is no cell wall or other structure for the drug to act on. Say that, rather than just *antibiotics don't work on viruses*.

why.matters: You meet pathogens every day, in every breath and on everything you touch, and you are ill perhaps a few times a year. That gap is the immune system, and most of it is not clever at all: skin, mucus, acid, and cells that eat anything foreign. The clever part, the lymphocytes that learn one pathogen and remember it, is what makes vaccination possible, and vaccination has removed one disease from the planet and made a dozen others rare. This topic gives the vocabulary the GCSE Health unit builds on: what a barrier is, what the two white blood cells do, why a vaccine works, and why an antibiotic cannot touch a cold.

examples.title: The scab on your knee
examples.body: Fall over, graze a knee, and every stage of this topic happens in one place over a week. The blood clots within minutes and the scab seals the gap. The skin round it goes red and warm because extra blood is bringing white blood cells. If bacteria got in, phagocytes engulf them and the yellow pus is what is left of both. Lymphocytes that match the bacteria multiply over the next few days, make antibodies, and clear the rest. When the scab falls off, memory cells for those bacteria are still in your blood.

visual.alt: A flow chart of a grazed knee: the clot and scab close the barrier, phagocytes engulf bacteria and leave pus, and any that remain are cleared by lymphocytes and antibodies, leaving memory cells

examples.title: The sore arm after a jab
examples.body: The day after a vaccination your arm aches and you may feel tired, and that is the lesson happening inside you. The vaccine put the pathogen's antigens into your arm. Phagocytes arrived first, which is the swelling. Then the rare lymphocytes that fit those antigens began multiplying, which takes energy and a few days, which is the tiredness. By the end of the week they have made antibodies and, more usefully, memory cells. You have had the first infection without the infection, and the sore arm was the price.

examples.title: Smallpox, from 1796 to 1980
examples.body: Smallpox killed about a third of the people who caught it and scarred most of the rest. In 1796 Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught cowpox from their cows did not catch smallpox, tested the idea on a boy, and the boy stayed well. Nobody knew why for another century. Once the mechanism was understood, the vaccine was taken round the world, and the virus ran out of people to infect. The last natural case was in 1977. In 1980 it was declared gone, the only human disease ever wiped out.

steps.title: How you get ill
steps.body:
The last topic sorted microbes into groups. This one is about what happens when a **pathogen** gets in, and how the body stops it.

**The sequence is always the same.** A pathogen finds a way in: breathed in, swallowed, through a cut, or carried by an insect. Inside, it finds warmth, moisture and food, and it **multiplies**. Bacteria double; viruses turn your cells into copying machines. As the numbers climb, the damage starts: bacteria release **toxins** that poison cells, and viruses **burst** the cells they have used. That damage is what you feel as **symptoms**.

**Some symptoms are the body fighting back**, not the pathogen. A **fever** is the body deliberately raising its temperature above the normal **37 °C**, to 38 °C or more, because many pathogens multiply more slowly when it is hotter and your own defence cells work faster. **Swelling** and redness round a cut are extra blood bringing white blood cells to the spot. A **runny nose** is mucus flushing pathogens out. Feeling terrible is often the sign that the defences are working.

**The time before symptoms** is the **incubation period**: the pathogen is multiplying but the numbers are still too small to notice. For a cold it is a day or two; for some diseases it is weeks, and a person can pass the pathogen on before they know they have it.

The body's defences come in **two lines**: stopping pathogens getting in at all, and dealing with the ones that do.

visuals.alt: A flow chart of an infection: the pathogen gets in, multiplies, releases toxins or bursts cells, and the outcome turns on whether the defences are winning, ending in recovery and immune memory

check.solution: Symptoms come from **damage**: the pathogen multiplies and either releases **toxins** or **bursts cells**. Fever and extra mucus are the body's own responses, not the pathogen's doing.

steps.title: The first line: keeping them out
steps.body:
Most pathogens never get in, because the body is sealed and armed at every entrance.

- **Skin** is a tough, dry layer that pathogens cannot get through. When it is cut, **platelets** in the blood make a **clot** that hardens into a **scab**, sealing the gap while new skin grows underneath.
- **Mucus** lines the nose, throat and airways. It is sticky and **traps** pathogens breathed in. **Cilia**, tiny hairs on the cells of the airway, beat to **sweep** the mucus up to the throat, where it is swallowed.
- **Hydrochloric acid** in the stomach, at about **pH 2**, kills most of the pathogens that arrive in food and drink, and in the swallowed mucus.
- **Tears** and **saliva** contain an enzyme, **lysozyme**, that breaks bacteria open.
- **Earwax** and **nose hairs** trap what floats in.

**These defences are general.** They stop any pathogen, without needing to recognise it. That makes them fast and cheap, and it is why a cut that is kept clean usually heals with no illness at all.

**Mucus and cilia are a pair**, and questions test that: the mucus **traps**, the cilia **move**. Smoke paralyses the cilia, so a smoker's mucus sits in the airways with its pathogens still in it, which is one reason smokers get more chest infections.

steps.title: The second line: white blood cells
steps.body:
A pathogen that gets past the barriers meets the **white blood cells**, and there are two kinds to know.

**Phagocytes** are the general troops. A phagocyte moves towards a pathogen, wraps itself round it and **engulfs** it, then **digests** it with enzymes. This is **phagocytosis**, and it works on anything foreign. The **pus** in an infected cut is mostly dead phagocytes and the bacteria they took with them.

**Lymphocytes** are the specialists. Every pathogen carries **antigens**, marker molecules on its surface, and each lymphocyte recognises **one** antigen. When a lymphocyte meets its antigen it multiplies and makes **antibodies**: proteins that fit that antigen and stick to it. Antibodies **clump** the pathogens together so phagocytes can engulf them faster, and mark them for destruction. Some lymphocytes also make **antitoxins**, which neutralise the toxins bacteria release.

**The difference in one line:** phagocytes attack anything, straight away; lymphocytes attack one thing, and take a few days to get going the first time.

**Why it takes a few days.** The lymphocyte that matches a new pathogen is rare, and it has to multiply before there are enough antibodies to make a difference. That is the gap between catching a cold and getting over it, and it is the gap that the next step closes.

steps.title: Immunity, and what a vaccine does
steps.body:
**Why you do not get chickenpox twice.** After an infection is beaten, some of the lymphocytes that matched it stay in the blood for years as **memory cells**. If the same pathogen returns, they recognise it at once and make antibodies **faster and in far larger amounts**, so it is destroyed before you feel ill. You are **immune**.

**A vaccine is that first meeting without the illness.** It contains a **dead or weakened** form of the pathogen, or just its antigens. It cannot cause the disease, but the antigens are real, so lymphocytes respond and memory cells form. The real pathogen, if it ever arrives, meets a body that has already practised.

**Where the idea came from.** In **1796** Edward Jenner, a country doctor, noticed that milkmaids who had caught **cowpox**, a mild disease from cows, never seemed to catch **smallpox**, which killed about a third of the people it infected. He scratched cowpox into the arm of a boy, James Phipps, and later exposed him to smallpox. The boy stayed well. The word *vaccine* comes from *vacca*, Latin for cow.

**Where it led.** Smallpox is the one human disease that has been wiped out. The last natural case was in **1977**, and in **1980** the World Health Organization declared it gone. No child born since has needed the vaccine.

**Vaccines protect other people too.** When most of a population is immune, a pathogen cannot find enough new hosts to keep spreading, so the few who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies, are protected as well. The GCSE unit calls this **herd immunity**.

steps.title: Antibiotics, and what they cannot do
steps.body:
**Antibiotics kill bacteria.** The first, **penicillin**, was found in **1928** by Alexander Fleming, who noticed a mould killing the bacteria round it on a dish he had left out. Antibiotics work by damaging parts a bacterial cell has and your cells do not, such as the **cell wall**, so the bacteria die and you are untouched.

**Antibiotics do nothing to viruses.** A virus is not a cell: no wall, no cytoplasm, nothing of its own for the drug to act on. Colds, flu, measles and chickenpox are viruses, so an antibiotic cannot help with any of them. The body's own immune response clears them, and a vaccine is the only medicine that helps in advance.

**Other medicines treat the symptoms, not the cause.** Paracetamol lowers a fever and eases pain; it does not touch the pathogen. A cough medicine soothes the throat. That is fine, as long as nobody mistakes feeling better for being cured.

**Finish the course.** An antibiotic kills the least resistant bacteria first. Stop early and the survivors are the ones that coped best with the drug; they multiply, and the next course works less well. That is how **antibiotic resistance** spreads, and it is a problem the GCSE Natural selection unit comes back to.

**Antiseptics are different again.** They are chemicals used **on skin and surfaces**, not inside the body, to kill microbes: the wipe before an injection, the spray on a kitchen counter.

steps.title: Four words that begin with anti
steps.body:
This topic has four words that start the same way and mean four different things, and mixing them up costs marks all through GCSE.

- An **antigen** is a marker molecule on the **surface of a pathogen**. It is what the immune system recognises. The pathogen has it; you do not make it.
- An **antibody** is a **protein made by a lymphocyte** that fits one antigen and sticks to it. You make it.
- An **antibiotic** is a **medicine that kills bacteria**. A drug, swallowed or injected, and useless against a virus.
- An **antiseptic** is a **chemical for skin and surfaces** that kills microbes on the outside of the body.

A way to keep them apart: *antigen* is the thing you are fighting against, *antibody* is what your body fights with, *antibiotic* is a medicine against living bacteria, *antiseptic* keeps things clean.

There is a fifth, less confusing: an **antitoxin** is an antibody-like protein that neutralises a toxin.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**General against specific.** The barriers and the phagocytes work on any pathogen and work at once; the lymphocytes work on one antigen and take days the first time. A grade 9 answer names which line it is describing, because the properties follow from it: general means fast but unable to learn, specific means slow the first time but remembered for ever.

**Why the second time is different.** After the first infection, memory lymphocytes for that antigen are already numerous, so the response starts at once and antibodies reach a high level before symptoms appear. A vaccine is that first infection arranged safely. The point most often missed: a vaccine gives **memory**, not a permanent supply of antibodies. Antibodies fade; memory cells stay.

**Antigen, antibody, antibiotic, antiseptic.** Four answers to four different questions. If a question says *the pathogen's surface*, the word is antigen. *Made by lymphocytes*: antibody. *Kills bacteria inside the body*: antibiotic. *Kills microbes on a surface*: antiseptic.

**Fever cuts both ways.** Raising the body to 38 °C slows many pathogens and speeds up the immune cells, so a mild fever is a defence, not a malfunction. But enzymes in your own cells have an optimum near 37 °C, and above about 40 °C they begin to stop working, which is why a high fever is treated.

**Finishing the course is natural selection.** An antibiotic kills the most susceptible bacteria first. Stopping early leaves the toughest survivors, which multiply and pass on whatever let them cope. Every unfinished course is a small selection experiment in favour of resistance.

**Jenner did not know why it worked.** Nobody knew about antigens or lymphocytes in 1796. He saw a pattern, tested it, and the result held. The explanation came a century later: an idea can be right and useful before its mechanism is understood, and that is worth saying when a question asks about the history.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A pathogen gets in, **multiplies**, and causes symptoms by releasing **toxins** or **bursting cells**; a **fever** above the normal 37 °C, swelling and a runny nose are the body fighting back.
- **First line, general**: skin and scabs, mucus that **traps** and cilia that **sweep**, stomach **hydrochloric acid** at about pH 2, **lysozyme** in tears and saliva.
- **Second line**: **phagocytes** engulf and digest any pathogen at once; **lymphocytes** recognise one **antigen** and make **antibodies** that stick to it, and **antitoxins**.
- **Pus** is dead phagocytes and pathogens. The first specific response takes **days**.
- **Memory lymphocytes** remain, so a second infection is met faster and harder: **immunity**.
- A **vaccine** is a dead or weakened pathogen, or its antigens: the first meeting without the illness. Jenner, cowpox and smallpox, **1796**; smallpox eradicated, **1980**.
- **Antibiotics** kill **bacteria** by damaging their cells; they do **nothing to viruses**. Finish the course, or the toughest bacteria survive.
- **Antigen** on the pathogen, **antibody** from a lymphocyte, **antibiotic** a medicine, **antiseptic** for skin and surfaces.

questions.solution: A fever is a **defence**: at 38 °C many pathogens multiply more slowly and the immune cells work faster. But your own enzymes have an optimum near 37 °C, and by about 40 °C they start to fail, so a high fever becomes a danger in itself and is brought down.

questions.prompt: Why can an antibiotic kill the bacteria in your body without killing your own cells?
questions.solution: A bacterial cell has a **cell wall**, which your cells do not have, and its ribosomes are a different kind from yours. An antibiotic that damages the wall, or targets the bacterial kind of ribosome, kills the bacterium and passes your cells by. That difference in cell structure is the whole reason antibiotics are possible.

questions.prompt: A new virus spreads through a town in the spring and again in the winter. In the winter, people who caught it in the spring hardly notice it. Why?
questions.solution: The spring infection left **memory lymphocytes** for that antigen. In the winter they respond at once, and antibody levels climb faster and higher than the first time, so the virus is beaten before it causes illness. Antibody levels themselves fade; memory does not. Phagocytes do not learn.

After three days the survivors are the ones that coped best; without the rest of the course they multiply, and pass on whatever helped them. Those resistant bacteria can infect other people, for whom the antibiotic then works less well.

questions.prompt: Some vaccines need a second dose months after the first. What is the point of the booster?
questions.solution: The first dose starts the response and leaves some memory cells. The booster is a **second meeting** with the antigens: the response is faster and larger, and it leaves **many more memory cells**, so immunity is stronger and lasts longer. Vaccines contain no live pathogen and add no antibodies.

markScheme.description: A second meeting with the antigens leaves far more memory cells, so protection is stronger and lasts longer

The second dose contains the live pathogen itself, which the first dose has prepared the body to survive safely
The booster adds antibodies directly to the blood
A second meeting with the antigens leaves far more memory cells, so protection is stronger and lasts longer

questions.prompt: A student cuts their finger on a rusty nail in the garden. Describe how the body responds, from the moment the skin is broken to the point where the student is immune to the bacteria involved.
questions.solution:
The nail breaks the **skin**, the body's main physical barrier, and soil bacteria get into the wound. The first response is to close the gap: **platelets** in the blood form a **clot**, which hardens into a **scab**, so that no more bacteria can enter while new skin grows underneath. The finger **swells** and feels warm, because extra blood is flowing to the cut and bringing white blood cells with it.

The **phagocytes** act first. They do not need to recognise the bacteria: a phagocyte moves towards anything foreign, **engulfs** it and **digests** it with enzymes. This is the general defence, and it starts within hours. Phagocytes die doing it, and the dead cells with the bacteria inside them collect as **pus**.

The **lymphocytes** are slower and more precise. The bacteria carry **antigens**, marker molecules on their surface, and only a few lymphocytes have receptors that fit them. Those lymphocytes **multiply** over several days and release **antibodies**, proteins shaped to fit the antigens. The antibodies stick to the bacteria and **clump** them, so phagocytes clear them faster, and some lymphocytes release **antitoxins** that neutralise the toxins the bacteria are releasing. This is why an infected cut takes days to settle: the specific response has to be built up from a handful of cells.

When the bacteria are gone, most of the lymphocytes die back, but some remain as **memory lymphocytes**. If the same bacteria ever enter again, those cells recognise the antigens at once and antibodies are made **faster and in far larger amounts**, before any symptoms develop. The student is **immune** to that pathogen, which is the same state a vaccine produces without the cut.

questions.prompt: A leaflet says: "If you are young and healthy, vaccines are pointless." Evaluate this claim.
questions.solution:
The claim misunderstands what a vaccine is for. A vaccine contains a **dead or weakened** form of a pathogen, or just its **antigens**. Lymphocytes respond to those antigens, make antibodies, and leave **memory lymphocytes** in the blood. If the real pathogen arrives, the memory cells make antibodies **fast and in bulk**, and the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms develop. Being young and healthy does not give anyone that memory in advance: immunity to a particular pathogen exists only after a first meeting with its antigens, and the vaccine is the safe way to have that meeting.

Healthy people **do** catch these diseases. A fit teenager who meets measles for the first time has no memory cells for it, and measles can cause pneumonia and brain damage in people who were perfectly well the week before. The healthiest immune system in the world still needs days to build its first specific response, and in those days a fast-moving pathogen can do serious harm.

The leaflet also ignores everyone else. A vaccinated person cannot pass the pathogen on, so when most of a population is immune the pathogen **cannot find enough new hosts** and stops spreading. That protects the people who cannot be vaccinated: newborn babies, people having chemotherapy, and those whose immune systems are too weak to respond. A healthy person who refuses a vaccine keeps a route open for the pathogen to reach them.

The evidence is **smallpox**. It killed about a third of those it infected, and it is gone: the last natural case was in **1977** and it was declared eradicated in **1980**, because enough people, healthy ones included, were vaccinated that the virus ran out of hosts. Vaccines are not pointless for the healthy; they are how the healthy protect themselves and everyone around them.

examTechnique.body:
Questions on this topic are marked on **vocabulary and sequence**. The vocabulary is the two white blood cells and the four anti-words, and one wrong word loses the mark however sound the sentence. The sequence is the order of a response: barrier, phagocytes, lymphocytes and antibodies, memory. *Describe* questions want that order; *explain* questions want the reason at each step, such as why the specific response takes days.

Two habits pay. **Name the line**: say whether a defence is general or specific, because its speed and its memory follow from that. And **finish the thought**: not *a vaccine contains a weakened pathogen* but *so lymphocytes respond and leave memory cells, without the illness*.
examinerErrors: Giving the trapping job to the **cilia**. The mucus traps; the cilia sweep it away.
Writing **antigen** for antibody, or **antibiotic** for antibody. The antigen is on the pathogen; the antibody is made by a lymphocyte; the antibiotic is a medicine.
Saying a vaccine contains **antibodies**, or leaves antibodies for life. It contains **antigens** and leaves **memory cells**.
Saying antibiotics treat a **cold** or **flu**. Both are viruses, and a virus is not a cell.
Describing the second response as *stronger* without saying **faster and larger**, or without naming **memory lymphocytes** as the reason.
Calling a fever a symptom of the pathogen rather than a **defence** the body switches on.
Muddling **phagocytes** and **lymphocytes**, or giving one cell both jobs.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer separates the general defences from the specific one and says why that matters: barriers and phagocytes act on anything and at once, lymphocytes act on one antigen, take days the first time, and leave memory. It puts a response in order without prompting. Asked about a vaccine it reaches for **memory lymphocytes**, not antibodies, and can say why a booster works and why the protection extends to people who were never vaccinated. It uses the four anti-words without hesitation, explains an antibiotic's selectivity through the **structure of a bacterial cell**, and treats an unfinished course as **natural selection** in miniature. And it can say, about Jenner, that an idea can work before anyone understands why.
